disease: Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies, brain anomalies, and seizures

messages.content: You are a clinical geneticist. You are given evidence about one rare disease and a cohort of patients described by HPO terms. Exactly one patient has the disease. Use only that evidence as your knowledge of the disease. Be explicit about which findings in the report drove each placement, and about findings that argue against it.

REPORT ON Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies, brain anomalies, and seizures (GTF3C3, OMIM:621201): # Phenotypic Identification and Clinical Differentiation of GTF3C3-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder (OMIM #621201) ## Cohort Overview and Reported Phenotypic Frequencies Neurodevelopmental disorder with dysmorphic facies, brain anomalies, and seizures (NEDFBS; OMIM #621201) is an ultrarare autosomal recessive entity caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in *GTF3C3*, which encodes a core subunit of the general transcription factor TFIIIC2 complex critical for RNA polymerase III (Pol III) transcription F3. Across worldwide clinical literature as of 2026, exactly 17 affected individuals have been molecularly and clinically characterized F1, F3. The primary characterization rests on two landmark series: the cohort of 12 individuals across 7 unrelated families reported by De Hayr et al. (2025; DOI: 10.1016/j.gim.2024.101253) and the series of 4 individuals across 3 unrelated families described by Abdel et al. / Abdel-Hamid et al. (2025; DOI: 10.1093/braincomms/fcaf055 / PMC11878552), with an additional comprehensive single patient review reported by López et al. (2026; DOI: 10.3389/fgene.2026.1860633) F1, F2, F3. ### Systematic Clinical Phenotype Frequencies | Phenotypic Finding (Exact Literature Wording) | Standard HPO Term | Cohort Frequency (Numerator / Denominator) | Percentage | Study Citation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Global developmental delay / intellectual disability | Global developmental delay (HP:0001263) / Intellectual disability (HP:0001249) | Abdel cohort: 4/4

(2026, DOI: 10.3389/fgene.2026.1860633) F4 | --- ## Discriminating Clinical and Neuroradiological Findings When evaluating a patient presenting with generalized neurodevelopmental delay, microcephaly, and seizures, clinical features vary in their discriminatory utility against overlapping disorders F1, F5. ### Ranked Discriminating Value 1. **Combined Progressive Cerebellar Atrophy and Frontal Lobe Hypoplasia (Highest Discrimination; Moderate-to-High Confidence)** *Phenotypic Presentation:* Structural neuroimaging reveals symmetric cerebellar atrophy—frequently involving the vermis and hemispheres—alongside anterior forebrain/frontal hypoplasia F8, F14. *Overlapping Disorders:* - *POLR3-related leukodystrophies (e.g., 4H syndrome):* Classically characterized by diffuse T2 hypomyelination, cerebellar atrophy, and hypodontia/hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. GTF3C3 presents with structural midline and lobar hypoplasia rather than diffuse white matter signal abnormality alone, though some myelin delay has been documented (Chapleau et al., 2026, DOI: 10.1038/s41582-026-01248-1) F5, F14. - *GTF3C5-related disorder:* Also disrupts TFIIIC/Pol III-mediated transcription and causes cerebellar atrophy and thinning of the corpus callosum; however, GTF3C5 presentation often emphasizes prominent leukoencephalopathy over primary frontal lobe hypoplasia (Iwata, 2024, DOI: 10.1007/s00439-024-02656-3) F15. *Confidence:* Moderate-to-High. The presence of marked frontal lobe hypoplasia in combination with progressive cerebellar volume loss strongly points toward GTF3C3 over other transcriptional or epileptic encephalopathies F8. 2. **Profound Expressive Speech Deficit Exceeding Motor Impairment (Intermediate Discrimination; Moderate Confidence)** *Phenotypic Presentation:* Affected children consistently present with absent or severely restricted speech, often completely non-verbal, accompanied by severe to profound cognitive disability F1. *Overlapping Disorders:* Differentiates from milder syndromic intellectual disabilities, though it overlaps significantly with severe epileptic encephalopathies (e.g., *ARX*-related West syndrome/epileptic encephalopathy) and *CDK19*-related neurodevelopmental disorder F1, F11. 3. **Craniofacial Dysmorphisms: Hypertelorism, Depressed Nasal Bridge, and Low-Set Ears (Low Discrimination; Low Confidence)** *Phenotypic Presentation:* Includes ocular hypertelorism (HP:0000316), broad or depressed nasal bridge (HP:0000425), and low-set ears (HP:0000369) F11. *Overlapping Disorders:* Highly indistinguishable from *CDK19*-, *ARX*-, or other Pol III/TFIIIC-related conditions on physical exam alone. Facial gestalt has generated conflicting interpretations regarding specificity F11, F17. 4. **Secondary Cortical Gyral Simplification (Poor Sensitivity; Low Discriminating Value)** *Phenotypic Presentation:* Simplified gyral pattern (HP:0009879) occurs in only 1 of 4 assessed individuals in the Abdel cohort and <30% overall F4, F8. Its presence reflects severe developmental compromise rather than a sensitive discriminator F4. --- ## Findings Looked for and Found Absent (Negative Predictors) In differential diagnosis, several negative findings provide clinical exclusion value: 1. **Intact Cognitive and Motor Development (HP:0001263 / HP:0001249)** Normal neurodevelopment has been consistently absent in confirmed individuals (0/16 in primary cohorts) F1, F9. The presence of mild developmental delay or normal cognitive milestones strongly argues against GTF3C3-related disorder F1, F9. 2. **Absence of Corpus Callosum Anomalies Cannot Rule Out Diagnosis** Importantly, agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum (HP:0001274 / HP:0002079) was present in only 7 of 16 (43.75%) evaluated individuals in the pooled review by López et al. (2026) F7. Therefore, clinicians **must not** exclude GTF3C3-related disorder on the basis of a structurally normal corpus callosum F7. 3. **Early Normal Brain MRI Does Not Exclude GTF3C3** While Abdel et al. (2025) and De Hayr et al. (2025) reported neuroimaging malformations in all evaluated patients, Papuc et al. (2019; DOI: 10.1038/s41431-018-0299-8) identified a patient with GTF3C3 involvement whose early cerebral MRI showed no identifiable malformations F9. Progressive neurodegenerative processes (cerebellar volume loss) emerge over chronological time, meaning a normal scan in early infancy does not rule out the disease F9. --- ## Phenotypic Variation by Variant Type, Position, Age, and Sex ### Variant Type and Functional Position - **Impact:** Functional studies suggest that biallelic loss-of-function variants or severe missense variants disrupting the TFIIIC complex assembly yield severe neurodevelopmental phenotypes F2. Zebrafish knockout models confirm disrupted motility and spontaneous seizure-like behavior upon loss of functional *gtf3c3* F16. - **Genotype-Phenotype Correlations:** Formal genotype-phenotype correlations are currently unestablished due to small sample sizes (17 total individuals) F2. Early hypotheses proposing that cortical malformations (simplified gyral pattern) are restricted to truncating/null alleles have been refuted: simplified gyral pattern was identified in individuals harboring missense alleles F18. ### Age-Dependent Phenotypic Evolution - **Seizure Emergence:** Seizures manifest early in life (infancy to early childhood), frequently evolving into refractory epilepsy F5, F6, F10. - **Neuroradiological Progression:** Midline cerebellar atrophy appears progressive; neurodegenerative changes become pronounced as children age, explaining why early scans may appear near-normal F8, F9. - **Facial Features Across Lifespan:** While Abdel et al. (2025) described facial dysmorphisms as recognizable in young children, longitudinal evidence shows that features in older individuals (up to 27 years of age) do not maintain a unique gestalt, confounding recognition in older adolescents and adults F11, F17. ### Sex-Specific Differences - The disorder affects both males and females across unrelated kindreds (e.g., affected sister pairs and affected males), consistent with standard autosomal recessive transmission F1, F10. No sex-limited penetrance or sex-dependent phenotypic severity has been identified F1, F2. --- ## Contested and Contradictory Literature Findings Several published observations exhibit direct friction across the literature: 1. **True Clinical Penetrance of Seizures (Deprioritised Finding [F10], [F12], [F13])** - *Contradiction:* Abdel et al. (2025) reported seizures in exactly 2 of 4 (50%) individuals gathered via GeneMatcher F6, F10. In contrast, De Hayr et al. (2025) reported seizures in 11 of 12 (91.7%) individuals F6, F12, and the pooled review by López et al. (2026) cited 82.4% penetrance F6. - *Underlying Cause:* While ascertainment bias (epileptic encephalopathy panels vs. general neurodevelopmental clinics) has been hypothesized to explain the discrepancy, De Hayr et al. primarily evaluated individuals for intellectual disability, yet observed >90% seizure rates F13. 2. **Distinct Facial Gestalt vs. Non-Specific Variable Features (Deprioritised Finding [F11], [F17])** - *Contradiction:* Abdel et al. (2025; PMC11878552) state that affected individuals exhibit a "distinctive dysmorphic facies that appear recognizable in very young children" F11, F17. Conversely, De Hayr et al. (2025) concluded that craniofacial features represent "variable nonfamilial facial features" that do not allow clinical diagnosis F11, F17. 3. **White Matter Pathology vs. Classical POLR3-Related Leukodystrophy (Deprioritised Finding [F14], [F15])** - *Contradiction:* Abdel et al. (2025) emphasized structural tissue loss (predominant cerebellar and frontal atrophy) as the hallmark F8, F14. However, Chapleau et al. (2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41582-026-01248-1) and Genomics England PanelApp document white matter abnormalities, including delayed myelination and demyelination, demonstrating that GTF3C3-related pathology bridges structural brain malformations and leukodystrophies F5, F14, F15. 4. **Obligate Brain Malformations at Initial Presentation (Deprioritised Finding [F9])** - *Contradiction:* In the series by Abdel et al. (2025) and De Hayr et al. (2025), 100% of imaged individuals exhibited identifiable structural abnormalities (cerebellar atrophy, frontal hypoplasia, or callosal dysgenesis) F8, F9. However, Papuc et al. (2019; DOI: 10.1038/s41431-018-0299-8) identified a confirmed case presenting with early-onset epileptic encephalopathy where cerebral MRI showed no overt malformations early on F9. --- ## Synthesis and Diagnostic Framework To pick an individual with GTF3C3-related disorder out of a cohort of patients with overlapping neurodevelopmental phenotypes: 1. **Core Triage Criteria:** The individual must display severe-to-profound global developmental delay/intellectual disability (100% penetrance) with severe expressive language deficit F1, F9. 2. **Neuroimaging Key Discriminator:** Look for symmetric progressive cerebellar atrophy combined with frontal lobe hypoplasia F8. Do not exclude the diagnosis if the corpus callosum is intact (present in only ~44% of cases) F7, or if cortical gyration is normal (simplified gyral pattern is seen in <30%) F4. 3. **Seizure Assessment:** Expect early-onset epilepsy in the majority (~80%) of patients, but recognize that ~20–50% of confirmed cases in non-epilepsy cohorts may lack seizures during early observation F6, F10, F12. 4. **Definitive Diagnosis:** Because facial features (hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge, low-set ears) heavily overlap with other TFIIIC-, CDK19-, and Pol III-related conditions F11, F15, phenotypic suspicion must be confirmed by identifying biallelic pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in *GTF3C3* via comprehensive exome or genome sequencing F2, F3. ## Sources 1. read.qxmd.com. ranking.for: Strongest match: primary microcephaly, severe global developmental delay/intellectual disability, seizures, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, agenesis of the corpus callosum, and simplified gyral pattern; the report identifies microcephaly, severe developmental impairment, epilepsy, cerebellar abnormalities, callosal anomalies, and occasional simplified gyration as compatible GTF3C3 findings.
ranking.against: The reported hallmark imaging combination of progressive cerebellar atrophy with frontal lobe hypoplasia is not documented; this patient instead has pontine/brainstem hypoplasia, severe visual impairment, dysphagia, and polyhydramnios, which are not characterized in the report.

ranking.for: Severe global developmental delay with major motor and language delay, secondary microcephaly, early severe epilepsy (focal-to-bilateral tonic-clonic seizures, spasms, and status), brain atrophy, and delayed CNS myelination align well with the report's core neurodevelopmental, epileptic, progressive neuroimaging, and white-matter spectrum.
ranking.against: No cerebellar atrophy or frontal lobe hypoplasia is specifically reported, and absent findings include myoclonic seizures; developmental regression, basal-ganglia/hippocampal abnormalities, ketosis, respiratory failure, and failure to thrive were not established features in the report.

ranking.for: Microcephaly, severe intellectual disability, multiple seizure types including myoclonic seizures, cerebellar atrophy, and corpus callosum hypoplasia constitute a highly concordant core phenotype; cerebellar atrophy plus a callosal anomaly is particularly supportive.
ranking.against: The report emphasizes severe expressive speech impairment/absent speech and global developmental delay, neither of which is recorded here, and frontal lobe hypoplasia is not documented; delayed puberty, macrodontia/diastema, choreoathetosis, and tetraparesis are not report-characteristic.

ranking.for: This patient has primary microcephaly, global developmental delay/intellectual disability, absent speech, seizures, hypotonia, and a thin corpus callosum, matching several highly recurrent clinical features in the report.
ranking.against: The key reported cerebellar atrophy/frontal hypoplasia combination is absent from the provided imaging, and recorded absence of corpus-callosum hypoplasia weighs somewhat against a callosal malformation despite the observed thin corpus callosum; optic nerve hypoplasia, growth-hormone deficiency, Chiari malformation, and periventricular nodular heterotopia are not described GTF3C3 features.

ranking.for: Severe intellectual disability, absent speech, profound motor impairment, motor seizures with EEG abnormality, hypotonia, and a thin corpus callosum fit the report's severe developmental, speech, epilepsy, and possible callosal-abnormality spectrum.
ranking.against: Recorded absence of microcephaly is less supportive, although not exclusionary across all reported cases; cerebellar atrophy and frontal lobe hypoplasia are not reported, while marked spasticity, self-mutilation, joint hypermobility, short stature, and low weight were not highlighted for GTF3C3 disorder.

rounds.what_the_report_lacked: Confidence would be improved by longitudinal MRI details for every candidate—specifically whether there is progressive symmetric cerebellar (vermis and hemispheric) atrophy and frontal lobe hypoplasia—plus head-growth trajectories, age at seizure onset and epilepsy course, formal expressive-language level, and targeted documentation of the reported facial features. Most importantly, the report provides no patient-level molecular data to assess whether a candidate has biallelic pathogenic or likely pathogenic GTF3C3 variants, which it states is required for definitive diagnosis.
